paper_metadata.title: On Aligning OpenIE Extractions with Knowledge Bases: A Case Study
paper_metadata.venue: Proceedings of the First Workshop on Evaluation and Comparison of NLP Systems (Eval4NLP)
paper_metadata.abstract: The paper directly and manually evaluates the information-content relationship between OPIEC OpenIE triples and DBpedia. It studies triples with the same arguments as DBpedia facts, then evaluates whether general OPIEC triples can be represented by one DBpedia fact or by KB formulas; it finds that one-fact mappings often lose specificity, while formulas express a substantial share of additional triples.

problem_addressed: The study examines the limits of aligning ambiguous, surface-relation OpenIE triples to semantically precise DBpedia facts and schemas. It tests the distant-supervision assumption for triples sharing an argument pair with a KB fact, and the implicit one-triple assumption that any OIE triple can be expressed by one KB fact.

methodology.description: Execution order: (1) start with OPIEC-Linked triples extracted by MinIE-SpaTe from English Wikipedia and retain linked, filtered, correctly extracted triples; (2) use DBpedia ontology facts with disambiguated entity arguments; (3) for the DSA study, find all DBpedia facts sharing an OPIEC triple's entity pair, present facts, types, and relation semantics to an annotator, label each hit as Same/OIE-More-Specific/KB-More-Specific/Different, and retain the best hit; (4) for the OTA study, generate candidates from KB-hit relation counts and then any domain/range-compatible DBpedia relation, label each triple Fully-/Partly-/Not-Expressible with one fact, and manually formulate multi-fact first-order formulas where they improve expressibility; (5) compare information presence in DBpedia; (6) rerun Stanford OIE, OpenIE 5, and RnnOIE on the sampled provenance sentences to assess transferability.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: DBpedia is both the reference KB and schema vocabulary. Candidate relations are constrained using DBpedia argument types and relation domain/range information; mapping-based DBpedia ontology triples are retained. The study also tests representation by conjunctive, existential, temporal, and disjunctive KB formulas rather than one fact.

input_output.input_type: Linked OpenIE triples (subject, surface relation, object) from English Wikipedia, their provenance sentences, and DBpedia facts, relation metadata, entity types, and schema vocabulary.
input_output.input_granularity: Individual linked OIE triples and entity pairs; transferability analyses rerun extractors on each sampled triple's provenance sentence.
input_output.output_representation: Per-triple semantic-alignment labels (Same, OIE-More-Specific, KB-More-Specific, Different); expressibility labels (Fully-, Partly-, Not-Expressible); and, where feasible, DBpedia facts or first-order logic KB formulas composed of DBpedia predicates.

DSA study samples: 100 correctly extracted non-Is-a triples with DBpedia KB hits and 100 correctly extracted Is-a OPIEC-Typed triples
OTA study sample: 100 correctly extracted linked OPIEC triples

evaluation.setting: Expert manual evaluation under an assumed perfect extractor and perfect OIE-to-KB alignments. In the DSA studies, annotators see every KB hit plus type and relation information and label the best semantic match. In the OTA study, annotators receive relation candidates from hit statistics or all type-compatible DBpedia relations, then assess best achievable one-fact expressibility and optionally formulate multi-fact formulas. Transferability is measured on matching-argument triples produced from the same provenance sentences by three OIE systems.

value: For non-Is-a triples with a DBpedia hit, 48% of best hits are Same, 40% OIE-More-Specific, 7% KB-More-Specific, and 5% Different; thus 88% allow the OIE triple to express its best hit.
For Is-a triples with a DBpedia hit, 36% are Same, 63% OIE-More-Specific, 0% KB-More-Specific, and 1% Different.

With hit-relation candidates only, 29% of sampled OPIEC triples are fully expressible by one DBpedia fact, 29% partly expressible, and 42% not expressible. With any type-compatible DBpedia relation, these are 42%, 41%, and 17%; with KB formulas, 66%, 20%, and 14%.
For information already present in DBpedia, 18% of sampled OPIEC content is fully present, 23% partly present, and 59% not present.

Across other extractors, hit-category label equivalence is 98% for Stanford OIE, 84% for OpenIE 5, 77% for RnnOIE, and 86% combined. Formula-expressibility equivalence is 98%, 89%, 89%, and 92%, respectively.

value: The paper directly evaluates information-content compatibility rather than relying only on downstream-task scores.
It separates semantic relatedness for existing same-argument KB hits from general expressibility, avoiding conflation of DSA and the one-triple assumption.
It evaluates both single-fact and compositional formula representations, showing where one-fact schema mapping loses information.
It includes a transferability check across three additional OIE extractors and analyzes entity/entity-pair overlap.

value: REVIEW-LEVEL INFERENCE: The manual samples (100 triples per stated sub-study) and expert-label procedure provide detailed semantic evidence but limit statistical precision and make annotation reproducibility dependent on undocumented annotator protocol details.

REVIEW-LEVEL INFERENCE: The conclusions are tied to English Wikipedia-derived OPIEC and DBpedia, and to filtered mapping-based DBpedia ontology facts; transfer to other domains, KB schemas, languages, and KB data models is not directly established.

REVIEW-LEVEL INFERENCE: Evaluation assumes correctly extracted, self-contained triples, correct argument disambiguation, and perfect best possible mappings, so it does not quantify end-to-end alignment performance under realistic extraction and linking errors.
